lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: Walk in Their Boots
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 1, Session 3
lesson.footer: Persuasive Writing | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 1 Session 3

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LA02 moving beyond bare assertions by taking account of differing ideas and opinions; VC2E5LE02 forming and sharing opinions on a literary text; VC2E5LY10 creating texts for purpose and audience
plan.shape: sort then become: a cut-and-paste sort of eight arguments, then a paragraph written in the voice of someone students disagree with, because writers who understand the other side argue better
plan.criticalFeature: who is speaking changes what they care about, and so what reason they give
decisionPoints: the Who might say it? round
the choice check: which reason would a scientist give?
the exit board: two voices on a new issue
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Today: every claim belongs to someone, and they have their reasons.
plan.catchUp: Missed Sessions 1-2? Say: an issue is a question fair people disagree on. They can do the sort and the paragraph today without the Issue Card.

routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: The issue written large: Should tourist boats take visitors to see polar bears?
A two-column chart: Who | What they care about

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: what each person cares about, whose words, fix the voice, then argue the other side.
resources.title: Walk in Their Boots
resources.subtitle: Who is speaking changes what they care about.

example.prompt: Issue: should the beach be closed to dogs? Person: a dog owner.
example.answer: A dog owner cares about walks and exercise, so they are against closing the beach.

items.prompt: Issue: should the beach be closed to dogs? Fill in each person.
answers: not being knocked over; or patting dogs
space to surf; maybe their own dog

example.prompt: 'The waves are better with no dogs in the water.' Who said it?
steps: Ask: what do they care about?

items.prompt: 'My customers love walking dogs past my shop.' Who said it?
'I keep swimmers safe from loose dogs.' Who said it?
'Dogs scare the birds off their nests.' Who said it?

example.prompt: As a ranger, I protect the birds. I personally love dogs though.
steps: Find the sentence in your own voice
Write what the ranger would say
example.answer: As a ranger, I protect the birds. Every nest matters to me.

items.prompt: Ava wrote as a lifeguard but slipped back into her own voice. Find it and fix it.
work: As a lifeguard, I worry about loose dogs near swimmers. Personally, I just think dogs are cute.
items.answer: The last sentence is Ava, not the lifeguard. Fix: Last summer I treated three children for dog scratches.

steps: Give the reason they care about most
example.answer: As a captain, I show visitors the Arctic. They go home and protect it. We stay far back and never feed the bears.

items.prompt: Tourist boats in the Arctic: choose a speaker from the side you DON'T agree with. Write their paragraph in their voice.
items.answer: Who I am, the reason they care about most, and an answer to the other side's worry.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: one fact told two ways, then a conversation where each side answers the other.
resources.title: Two Voices
resources.subtitle: Same facts, different eyes.

example.prompt: Fact: 40 tour boats visited the bay last summer.
steps: How would the captain tell it?
How would the scientist tell it?
example.answer: Captain: 40 boats of people who now care about bears! Scientist: 40 boats of noise in the bears' hunting grounds.

items.prompt: Write how each person would tell the same fact.
rows: The tour season is now twice as long.
Visitors take 10,000 photos of bears a year.
The town has a new tour office.
answers: The tour season is now twice as long.
More months of jobs and learning
Visitors take 10,000 photos of bears a year.
The town has a new tour office.

example.prompt: Captain: People who see bears protect them. Scientist: ...
steps: Start with the captain's best reason
The scientist answers that exact reason
example.answer: Scientist: People can care through cameras, without boats in the way.

items.prompt: Write a short conversation (6 lines) between the captain and the scientist. Each line must answer the one before.
items.answer: Six lines; each answers the line before; both voices stay fair.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: Supported option: a short sort, a partly filled chart and a paragraph frame.
resources.title: Walk in Their Boots Helper
resources.subtitle: Ask: who are they, and what do they care about?

steps: Does it want boats or not?

items.prompt: Sort the cards: FOR or AGAINST tourist boats.
items.hint: FOR cards say something good about the boats.

example.answer: jobs and showing people the Arctic

items.prompt: Fill in what each person cares about.
answers: seeing a bear once in a lifetime
items.hint: The first one is done for you.

example.answer: As a bear scientist, I care about where bears hunt. That is why I worry about boats.

items.prompt: Choose one person. Finish the frame: As a ___, I care about ___. That is why I ___.
items.answer: A three-part paragraph in that person's voice.
items.hint: Use I and my, as if you are them.

resources.label: Perspective Cards
resources.description: Cut-and-paste activity: eight arguments about Arctic tourist boats, in mixed order. One sheet per student.
resources.title: Perspective Cards
resources.subtitle: Cut out the cards. Sort them FOR or AGAINST on your mat.

cards.text: Visitors who see a polar bear up close go home and fight to protect them.
Boats bring noise and fuel into the places where bears hunt.
Tourism pays for the jobs that keep our small Arctic town alive.
This is the bears' home, not a zoo. They were here first.
A bear that gets used to people can become a danger to them, and to itself.
Every ticket sold can help pay for polar bear research.
Every flight and cruise to the Arctic adds to the warming that melts the ice.
Seeing a wild polar bear is a once-in-a-lifetime memory.

resources.tip: Stretch: star the strongest card on each side. Write why it is the strongest.

resources.label: Perspective Sort Mat
resources.description: Glue mat for the Perspective Cards: FOR and AGAINST boxes and a bank of speakers to label each card.
resources.title: Should tourist boats take visitors to see polar bears?
resources.subtitle: Glue each card on the side it argues for. Under each card, write who might say it.

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today we step into other people's boots and argue their side.

Print one Perspective Cards sheet and one Sort Mat per student for the cut and paste. Then the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for students who need it. Scissors and glue on tables.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to see an issue through other people's eyes.
successCriteria: I can say who cares about an issue and why.
I can sort arguments for and against and name who might give them.
I can write a paragraph from a point of view that is not my own.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Today you argue a side you might not even agree with.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Naming who cares is where everyone starts.
Sorting and naming the speaker is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 naming who cares is reachable for all; SC2 sorting and naming the speaker is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 writing in another voice is the stretch most students will reach.

slides.title: Same news, different eyes
lines: The canteen is closing for a week.
How does it feel for the canteen worker? A student who forgot lunch? A parent?

notes.answer: worried about pay; hungry and cross; relieved or annoyed
beats: SAY: One piece of news. Three people hear it.
Same news, different feelings.
ASK: Is the canteen closing good news or bad news?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: a mix. That's the point.
ASK: Pick one person. How do they feel about the canteen closing, and why?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: the worker is worried about money; the student is hungry
SAY: Who you are changes what you care about.
In The Last Bear, April and her dad see Bear Island differently too.
trap: Fix: ask what does this person lose or win? Student answers for that person.
notes.prep: Low-coupling launch: everyone can reason about the canteen, so returning students join fully. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: The way one person sees an issue, because of who they are.
slides.example: From a farmer's perspective, rain is great. From a camper's, not so much.

notes.answer: the way one person sees an issue, because of who they are
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Perspective. Say it with me. Perspective.
SAY: Your perspective is how you see something because of who you are.
Same rain. The farmer cheers, the camper groans.
ASK: From a dog's perspective, what is the best part of the day?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: walk time, dinner time
trap: thinking perspective means opinion, with no reason why.
Fix: ask because of who they are? Student adds the who.
notes.prep: Point of view in plain words. The binoculars: you look from where someone stands.

slides.title: Step into their boots
lines: Should tourist boats take visitors to see polar bears?
Who are they? What do they care about? So which side?

notes.answer: the captain cares about jobs, so for; the scientist cares about hunting grounds, so against
beats: POINT to the question.
SAY: Here's today's issue. I'll step into two pairs of boots.
POINT to Boat captain.
SAY: I drive the boat. My crew needs this job.
I love showing people the Arctic. So I'm for the boats.
POINT to Bear scientist.
SAY: I study where bears hunt. Noise and fuel worry me.
So I'm against.
ASK: Same issue. Why do they disagree? One word.
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: they care about different things; jobs, bears
trap: deciding the side first, then inventing a reason.
Fix: student answers who? and cares about? before choosing a side.
notes.stretch: Find something the captain and scientist both care about.
notes.help: Use the three questions on the slide in order.
notes.prep: The model. Critical feature: who is speaking changes what they care about, and so the reason they give.

slides.title: Who might say it?
slides.pivot: ask: what does this person win or lose?
slides.followUp: cold call one board: what words gave them away?

items.text: If the boats stop, I lose my job.
My tracking data shows bears avoid busy waters.
I saved for ten years to make this trip.
Leave me alone so I can hunt in peace.
items.say: The bear itself. Writers can speak for an animal too. Tick or fix.

say: Four quotes. Write who might say it, and which side.
Look for the clue in what they care about.
trap: writing only for or against, with no speaker.
Fix: student writes the who first, then the side.
notes.stretch: Name a second person who might say the same thing.
notes.help: Choose from: scientist, captain, tourist, ranger, polar bear.
notes.prep: Guided practice on new quotes before the cards. SC2.

slides.title: Which reason would a bear scientist most likely give?

options.text: Tickets bring good money into town.
options.misconception: gives the captain's or business view, not the scientist's

options.text: Boats can disturb bears while they hunt.

options.misconception: gives the tourist's view; ignores who is speaking

notes.answer: B - boats can disturb bears while they hunt
beats: SAY: You are the scientist now. Think about what you study.
ASK: Which reason would a bear scientist most likely give?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: who would give reason A?
Less -> fill the Who / Cares about chart, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. A scientist cares about how the bears live, so that's their reason.
trap: choosing the reason they personally agree with.
Fix: ask what does a scientist study? Student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Decision point before the cut-and-paste. Under 80% means the first two cards are sorted together.

slides.title: Cut, sort, glue
lines: Sort them FOR or AGAINST, then glue.
Write who might say it under each card.

notes.answer: FOR: protect, jobs, research, memory. AGAINST: noise, their home, danger, warming
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Sort before you glue. Lay all eight out first, then decide.
SAY: Cut, sort, label. Say it with me.
3 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: Before gluing: the jobs card. For or against?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, 1 for, 2 against... show me.
EXPECT: 1, for
CIRCULATE. Ask one student per table: who would say that card?
ASK: Hold up the card you think is strongest on your side.
5 sec. Cue: Hold it up, voices off... show me.
EXPECT: any card, held up with a reason ready
trap: gluing before sorting, then getting stuck.
Fix: student lays all cards out, sorts, then glues.
notes.prep: Fun activity: cut and paste. 12 minutes. The sorted mat becomes the reason bank for the paragraph. SC2.
notes.stretch: Star the strongest card each side; write why.
notes.help: Sort with a partner, then label on your own.

slides.title: Write in their voice
slides.extract: As a tour boat captain, I have shown thousands of visitors the Arctic. Every one of them goes home changed. They donate, they vote and they tell their friends. My boat follows strict rules: we stay far back, we cut the engine and we never feed the bears.
highlights: Every one of them goes home changed

notes.answer: say who you are, give the reason they care about, answer the other side's worry
beats: READ it aloud once, like the captain.
SAY: I'm writing as someone else, so I start by saying who I am.
POINT to goes home changed.
SAY: Then the reason this person cares about most.
POINT to we stay far back.
SAY: A clever captain answers the scientist's worry before they can say it.
ASK: What are the three moves I made?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: who I am, why I care, answer the worry
trap: switching back to their own view halfway through.
Fix: student reads it aloud as the character and crosses out their own opinion.
notes.stretch: Write the scientist's reply in the same three moves.
notes.help: Use the frame: As a ___, I believe ___ because ___.
notes.prep: Second model, for the You Do: who I am, why I care, answer the worry. SC3.

slides.title: Argue the other side
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet. Finish by arguing the other side, in their voice.

beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: This is the hard one.
Argue for the side you disagree with, as well as you can.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Read the first line: is it clearly someone else's voice?
TIME 12 minutes. At 9 minutes, two students read theirs in character.
trap: a weak paragraph on purpose, because they disagree.
Fix: ask would this person be proud of it? Student strengthens one reason.
notes.stretch: Extension: one fact told two ways, and a conversation where each side answers.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: a short sort, a partly filled chart, a paragraph frame.
notes.prep: Independent application. The other side's best reason is what students rebut in tomorrow's debate. SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in a paragraph written in the voice of a speaker from the other side

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Should the school ban ball games at lunch?
Write what a Prep student might say, and what a teacher on yard duty might say.

notes.answer: two different reasons: Prep loves the games; teacher worries about kids getting hit
beats: SAY: A brand new issue, two new people. Show me both perspectives.
ASK: Write one sentence for each person.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: two different reasons that fit who is speaking
RECORD who gives both people the same reason. Tomorrow's debate partners.
trap: both sentences in the student's own voice.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new issue: naming what each speaker cares about. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Did arguing the other side change your mind at all? Tell your partner why or why not.

notes.answer: open - listen for students who now see a reason on the other side
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can argue someone else's side?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Did arguing the other side change your mind at all?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: a bit, because their reason about jobs made sense
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. Collect the Sort Mats; they are the reason bank for tomorrow's debate. SC2.
